output: go version prints the release of the go toolchain installed on your machine, which matters when code needs a newer language feature

input: what does go clean do
output: go clean removes files the go command created; flags like -cache or -testcache clear just one cache, and plain go clean removes binaries built by go build

input: what does go list show
output: go list prints information about your code; go list ./... shows the local units of code and go list -m all shows every module in the dependency graph

input: what does go mod download fetch
output: go mod download fetches the modules listed in go.mod into the local module cache without building anything, so later builds work offline

input: what does go mod verify check

input: what does go mod graph do

input: how does go vet differ from go test
output: go vet analyzes your code for suspicious patterns without running it, while go test compiles and runs your tests and reports pass or fail for each set of tests

input: how does gofmt differ from go vet
output: gofmt only rewrites your source into the standard format, while go vet analyzes what the code means and warns about likely bugs that formatting cannot catch

input: how does go get differ from go install
output: go get adds or upgrades a dependency in your module, while go install builds a program and places the resulting binary in your bin directory

input: what does gofmt's l flag list
output: the l flag makes gofmt list the files whose formatting differs instead of rewriting them, which is how you check formatting in scripts

input: what does gofmt's w flag rewrite
output: the w flag makes gofmt rewrite each file in place with the standard formatting

input: what does go test print with -v

input: what does go test's -run option select
output: the run flag takes a name pattern and runs only the matching tests, which is how you run a single test out of a whole suite

input: what does go test's -cover option measure
output: the cover flag makes go test report what fraction of your statements the tests exercised, printed as a percentage

input: what does go build's o flag name
output: the o flag sets the name and location of the binary that go build writes, instead of using the default name from the directory

input: what does go doc display

input: how do i print formatted text in go
output: Use fmt.Printf with verbs like %s for strings, %d for integers, and %v for any value. Println adds spaces and a newline, while Sprintf returns the formatted string instead of printing it.

input: what is the difference between Printf and Sprintf
output: Printf writes formatted text to standard output, while Sprintf returns it as a string. Use Sprintf when you need to build a message to store or pass along rather than print.

input: how do i check if a string contains another string in go
output: Use strings.Contains, which returns true when the substring appears inside the string. There are also HasPrefix and HasSuffix for checking how a string starts or ends.

input: how do i split a string in go
output: Use strings.Split to break a string into a slice on a separator, or strings.Fields to split on any whitespace. Join the pieces back together with strings.Join.

input: how do i replace text in a string in go
output: Use strings.ReplaceAll to swap every occurrence, or strings.Replace with a count to limit replacements. Strings are immutable, so these return a new string.

input: how do i trim whitespace from a string in go
output: Use strings.TrimSpace to remove leading and trailing whitespace. Trim cuts specific characters from both ends, while TrimPrefix and TrimSuffix remove one exact affix.

input: how do i convert a string to a number in go
output: Use strconv.Atoi for plain integers, or strconv.ParseInt and ParseFloat when you need a specific size or base. They return an error if the text is not a valid number.

input: how do i convert a number to a string in go
output: Use strconv.Itoa for integers, or strconv.FormatInt and FormatFloat for other numeric kinds. Avoid adding numbers to strings directly, since that will not compile.

input: how do i read a file line by line in go
output: Open the file with os.Open, then wrap it in a bufio.Scanner and loop with Scan and Text. Always close the file with defer right after opening it.

input: how do i write text to a file in go
output: Use os.WriteFile with the filename, the content as bytes, and permission bits like 0644. It creates the file if missing and replaces its contents otherwise.

input: how do i read an environment variable in go
output: Use os.Getenv to read a variable, which returns an empty string when unset. Use os.LookupEnv when you must tell apart an empty value from a missing one.

input: how do i exit a go program with an error code
output: Call os.Exit with a nonzero status like 1 to signal failure. Note that deferred calls do not run on os.Exit, so clean up first.

input: how do i create a folder in go
output: Use os.MkdirAll to create a directory and any missing parents. It returns nil when the directory already exists, so it is safe to call repeatedly.

input: how do i get the current working directory in go
output: Call os.Getwd, which returns the directory path and an error. Command-line tools often use it to resolve relative file paths.

input: what are the Reader and Writer interfaces in go
output: Reader has one method, Read, for pulling bytes from a source, and Writer has Write for pushing bytes out. Files, network connections, and buffers all implement them, so they compose well.

input: how do i copy data from one stream to another in go
output: Use io.Copy with a Writer destination and a Reader source. It streams the bytes efficiently without loading everything into memory at once.

input: how do i throw away output in go
output: Write to io.Discard, a Writer that drops everything it receives. It is handy when an API requires a Writer but you do not need the data.

input: when should i use bufio in go
output: Use bufio when reading or writing in small pieces, since it batches operations and reduces slow system calls. It is ideal for line-by-line file or network input.

input: what is a bytes Buffer used for in go
output: A bytes.Buffer collects bytes in memory and implements both Reader and Writer. It is useful for building up output before writing it somewhere.

input: how do i fetch a web page in go
output: Use http.Get with the URL, then read and close the response body. Always close the body, even on errors, or connections will leak.

input: how do i handle web requests in go
output: Register a handler with http.HandleFunc giving a path pattern and a function that receives the response writer and request. Then start the server with http.ListenAndServe.

input: what is an http ServeMux in go
output: A ServeMux routes incoming requests to handlers based on URL patterns. The default one is used by http.HandleFunc, but you can create your own for cleaner routing.

input: how do i set an http header in go
output: Set headers on the request or response with Header().Set before the body is written. Response headers must be set before the first write.

input: how do i send a 404 response in go
output: Call http.NotFound with the writer and request, or use WriteHeader with any status code. WriteHeader must come before writing the body.

input: how do i turn a struct into json in go
output: Use json.Marshal, which returns the JSON bytes and an error. Field names become the keys unless you add json tags to rename them.

input: how do i parse json into a struct in go
output: Use json.Unmarshal with the JSON bytes and a pointer to your struct. Unknown fields are ignored, and missing fields keep their zero values.

input: how do i rename json fields in go
output: Add a tag like json:"user_name" to the struct field. The tag json:"-" skips a field entirely, and omitempty drops empty values.

input: when should i use a json Decoder instead of Unmarshal
output: Use json.Decoder for streams, like reading multiple JSON values from a network connection. Unmarshal is simpler for a single JSON document already in memory.

input: how do i get the current time in go
output: Call time.Now, which returns the local date and time. Use time.Since with a start value to measure how long something took.

input: how do i pause a go program for a second
output: Call time.Sleep with a duration like time.Second. Durations multiply, so 500 * time.Millisecond means half a second.

input: how do i parse a date string in go
output: Use time.Parse with a layout built from the reference time Mon Jan 2 15:04:05 MST 2006. The layout must use that exact reference date, not a pattern like YYYY-MM-DD.

input: how do i format a date in go
output: Call Format on the time value with a layout based on the reference time 01/02 03:04PM 2006. The layout "2006-01-02" produces year-month-day output.

input: what is the difference between a Timer and a Ticker in go
output: A Timer fires once after a duration, while a Ticker fires repeatedly on an interval. Stop both when done so they do not leak resources.

input: how do i run something after a delay in go
output: Use time.After, which returns a channel that receives one value after the duration. It is often paired with select to add timeouts.

input: how do i sort a slice in go
output: Use sort.Slice with the slice and a less function describing the order. For strings or ints there are also the simpler sort.Strings and sort.Ints helpers.

input: how do i check if a slice is already sorted in go
output: Use sort.SliceIsSorted or sort.IntsAreSorted to test without changing anything. They return true when every element is in order.

input: when should i use errors New in go
output: Use errors.New for a fixed, unchanging error message. When the message needs values from the situation, use fmt.Errorf instead.

input: how do i check for a specific error in go
output: Use errors.Is to test whether an error matches a known sentinel, even through wrapping. Comparing errors with == misses wrapped cases.

input: how do i get details out of an error in go
output: Use errors.As to extract a specific error kind from a wrapped chain into a variable of that kind. It reports whether the conversion succeeded.

input: how do i combine multiple errors in go
output: Use errors.Join to merge several errors into one that still matches each part with errors.Is and errors.As. It returns nil when given no errors.

input: what does the log package do in go
output: The log library prints timestamped messages for diagnostics. log.Fatal prints a message and exits, while a custom Logger lets you control the prefix and destination.

input: what is slog in go
output: slog provides structured logging with key-value pairs instead of plain text. It ships with text and JSON output handlers.

input: how do i match a pattern in a string in go
output: Compile a pattern with regexp.Compile, then use MatchString to test or FindString to extract. Regexp is powerful but slower than the strings library for simple checks.

input: how do i build a file path in go
output: Use filepath.Join to combine path pieces with the correct separator for the operating system. Never concatenate paths with slashes by hand.

input: how do i list all files in a folder in go
output: Use filepath.WalkDir with the root and a function called for each file or directory found. It visits nested folders automatically.

input: how do i get a file extension in go
output: Use filepath.Ext to get the suffix like .go, and filepath.Base for the final name in a path. filepath.Dir returns everything except that final name.

input: how do i run another program from go
output: Use the os/exec library to build a command with its name and arguments, then call Run or Output. Arguments are passed directly, never through a shell.

input: how do i listen for network connections in go
output: Use net.Listen with the network kind like tcp and an address such as localhost:8080. Accept then waits for each incoming connection in turn.

input: how do i hash data in go
output: Use the crypto/sha256 library to digest bytes into a fixed-size checksum. For non-security uses like hash tables, the faster fnv library is enough.

input: how do i encode data as base64 in go
output: Use base64.StdEncoding.EncodeToString for bytes that must travel as text. Decode with DecodeString, which reports an error on invalid input.

input: how do i read a csv file in go
output: Use the encoding/csv Reader on the file to get each row as a slice of strings. It handles quoted fields and commas inside quotes for you.

input: how do i convert bytes to a hex string in go
output: Use hex.EncodeToString to render bytes as readable hexadecimal. DecodeString converts back and errors on malformed input.

input: how do i generate random numbers in go
output: Use math/rand for simulations and games, seeding it for repeatable results. For passwords or tokens, use crypto/rand, which is secure but slower.

input: how do i count characters in a go string
output: Use utf8.RuneCountInString, because len counts bytes and multibyte characters inflate it. Ranging over a string also yields one rune at a time.

input: how do i include a file inside my go binary
output: Use the embed library with a go:embed comment above a string or byte-slice variable naming the file. The file content is then baked into the binary.

input: how do i read everything from a stream in go
output: Use io.ReadAll on a Reader to collect all bytes into a slice. Only use it when the input size is bounded, or memory can blow up.

input: how do i make an http request with a timeout in go
output: Create an http.Client with a Timeout field, then call its Get or Do methods. The default client has no timeout and can hang forever.

input: how do i send json to a web server in go
output: Use http.Post with the URL, a JSON content kind like application/json, and the body as a Reader. Read and close the response body afterward.

input: how do i parse a url in go
output: Use url.Parse from net/url to split a URL into scheme, host, path, and query parts. Query values come back as a map of string slices.

input: how do i generate html safely in go
output: Use html/template, which escapes values automatically to prevent injection attacks. The text/template sibling does no escaping and suits non-HTML output.

input: when should i use sync Map in go
output: Use sync.Map when many goroutines read and write a map with keys that change over time. For simple cases, a plain map guarded by a mutex is clearer.

input: what is sync Pool for in go
output: A sync.Pool recycles temporary objects to reduce garbage-collector pressure. Get borrows one and Put returns it, but the pool may drop items at any time.

input: how do i safely increment a counter from goroutines
output: Use atomic.AddInt64 on a shared int64, or a mutex around a plain increment. Atomics are faster for single values; mutexes suit groups of fields.

input: how do i cancel work after a deadline in go
output: Create a context with context.WithTimeout and pass it down; its Done channel closes at the deadline. Always call the returned cancel function to free resources.

input: should i put data in a context in go
output: Only put request-scoped values like IDs or tokens in a context, using unexported key kinds. Never store optional function parameters there; pass those explicitly.

input: how do i accept command line flags in go
output: Use the flag library to declare string, int, or bool flags, then call flag.Parse. Values arrive as pointers, or use the Var forms with your own variables.

input: how do i handle ctrl c in a go program
output: Use signal.Notify to route interrupt signals into a channel, then wait on it before shutting down. This lets you clean up instead of dying instantly.

input: how do i find how many cpus a machine has in go
output: Call runtime.NumCPU from the runtime library. The scheduler uses this count by default to run goroutines in parallel.

input: how do i detect the operating system in go
output: Check runtime.GOOS, which holds values like linux, darwin, or windows. For file paths, prefer filepath, which adapts automatically.

input: what is the difference between errors New and fmt Errorf
output: errors.New makes a fixed message, while fmt.Errorf formats one with values and can wrap another error with %w. Use fmt.Errorf when context matters.

input: how do i safely quote a string in go
output: Use strconv.Quote to produce a double-quoted, escaped representation. It is useful for debug output and generating valid Go string literals in text.

input: what is the difference between path and filepath in go
output: The path library always uses forward slashes and suits URLs, while path/filepath uses the operating system's separator and suits real files.

input: how do i write to two places at once in go
output: Use io.MultiWriter to fan out every write to several Writers, like a file and the terminal. A single Write call reaches all of them.

input: how do i read only the first n bytes in go
output: Wrap the Reader with io.LimitReader to cap how much can be read. It protects against unexpectedly huge inputs.

input: how do i match url methods in go http routing
output: Newer ServeMux patterns can include the method, like "GET /users/{id}", with path values read from the request. Older code often used a third-party router instead.

input: how do i stream json output in go
output: Use json.NewEncoder on a Writer and call Encode for each value. Each call writes one complete JSON value followed by a newline.

input: why should i stop a ticker in go
output: An unstopped ticker keeps its goroutine and channel alive, leaking resources. Always defer a call to Stop when the ticker is no longer needed.

input: what is fan in in go
output: Fan-in merges several channels into one by starting a goroutine per input that forwards values. It lets many producers feed a single consumer.

input: what is a pipeline in go
output: A pipeline chains stages where each stage reads from one channel and writes to the next. Data flows through, and each stage can run concurrently.

input: how do i add a timeout to a channel receive in go
output: Use select with the channel case plus a time.After case for the deadline. Whichever fires first wins, so slow operations do not hang you.

input: what is a done channel in go
output: A done channel is closed to broadcast cancellation to every goroutine selecting on it. Closing wakes all waiters at once, unlike sending one value.

input: how do i collect errors from goroutines in go
output: Give each goroutine a way to report back, like an error channel or a shared slice guarded by a mutex, then wait for all of them before checking results.

input: how do i limit how many goroutines run at once
output: Use a buffered channel as a semaphore: send a token before starting work and release it when done. Only as many goroutines proceed as the buffer holds.

input: what is the or done pattern in go
output: Or-done wraps a channel read so it also stops when a done channel closes. It prevents goroutines from blocking forever on a channel nobody will feed.

input: how do i rate limit requests in go
output: Use a time.Ticker to release work at a steady pace, or a token bucket channel refilled on an interval. Each request waits for a token before proceeding.

input: what is a heartbeat in go concurrency
output: A heartbeat is a periodic signal on a channel proving a goroutine is still alive. The supervisor watches it and can restart work that goes silent.

input: what is a generator in go
output: A generator is a function that starts a goroutine producing values on a returned channel. The caller ranges over the channel to consume them lazily.

input: how do i do a non blocking channel send in go
output: Use select with a send case and a default case. If no receiver is ready, the default runs immediately instead of waiting.

input: why should only the sender close a channel
output: Closing from the receiver side risks a panic if a sender still writes, since sends on a closed channel panic. The sender knows when no more values are coming.

input: what happens if you close a closed channel in go
output: The program panics. Guard with sync.Once or restructure so exactly one owner closes the channel.

input: what happens when you send on a closed channel
output: The program panics immediately. Receives on a closed channel are safe and return zero values once drained, but sends are not.

input: what does a nil channel do in go
output: Sends and receives on a nil channel block forever. In a select, a nil channel case is simply disabled, which is useful for toggling branches.

input: what happens with select when no case is ready
output: Select picks randomly among ready cases, or blocks until one becomes ready. Add a default case to avoid blocking, or a timeout case to bound the wait.

input: is select fair in go
output: When several cases are ready, select chooses one uniformly at random. It does not prefer the first listed case.

input: how do i break out of a for select loop in go
output: Use a labeled break, since a plain break only exits the select. Alternatively, return from the function or close over a done flag.

input: what is an empty select in go
output: A select with no cases blocks forever. It is occasionally used to park the main goroutine, though waiting on a signal channel is clearer.

input: how do i wait for the first of several tasks to finish
output: Start each task in a goroutine sending its result to one shared channel, then take the first receive. Cancel the losers with a context so they do not leak.

input: how do i run tasks and keep their results in order
output: Tag each task with its index, collect results on a channel, and place each into a slice by index. Concurrency scrambles arrival order, so track positions yourself.

input: how do i shut down a go server gracefully
output: Listen for an interrupt signal, then call the server Shutdown method with a timeout context. In-flight requests finish while new ones are refused.

input: how do i stop a worker pool cleanly in go
output: Close the jobs channel so workers exit their range loops, then wait on a WaitGroup. Results can be collected before or after the wait.

input: how do i handle a producer faster than its consumer
output: Use a buffered channel sized for bursts, drop or sample when full with select-default, or slow the producer with rate limiting. Unbounded queues just move the crash to memory.

input: how do i retry with backoff in go
output: Loop the attempt, sleeping an increasing duration between tries, often with jitter. Give up after a max count or when a context is canceled.

input: how does a buffered channel act as a semaphore
output: Sending into a buffered channel of size n blocks once n tokens are held, so at most n goroutines proceed. Receiving a token releases one slot.

input: how do i share a read heavy value safely
output: Use a sync.RWMutex so many readers proceed together while writers get exclusive access. For a single value, atomic operations are even cheaper.

input: when is sync Map better than a mutex
output: sync.Map shines when keys are written once and read often by many goroutines. A plain map with a mutex is simpler and faster for most other cases.

input: how do i broadcast to many goroutines at once
output: Close a shared done channel; every goroutine selecting on it wakes immediately. For repeated broadcasts, use sync.Cond or a fresh channel per round.

input: what is sync Cond used for
output: A sync.Cond lets goroutines wait until a condition becomes true, then wakes one or all of them. Always re-check the condition in a loop after waking.

input: why must WaitGroup Add happen before starting goroutines
output: Add sets the counter that Done decrements, so it must run before any goroutine might call Done. Adding inside the goroutine races with Wait.

input: why should you not copy a WaitGroup
output: Copying a WaitGroup duplicates its internal counter, so Done calls hit the wrong copy and Wait may return early. Always pass it by pointer.

input: what does go vet copylocks check
output: It flags copying values that contain a lock, like a mutex or WaitGroup, since the copy shares no state with the original. Pass locks by pointer instead.

input: how do i detect a goroutine leak
output: Watch runtime.NumGoroutine grow over time, or take a goroutine stack dump with SIGQUIT. Leaks usually come from goroutines blocked on channels nobody reads.

input: how do i get a goroutine stack dump
output: Send SIGQUIT to the process, or set GOTRACEBACK to control the detail. The dump shows what every goroutine is blocked on.

input: can go use multiple cpu cores
output: Yes, the scheduler runs goroutines on multiple threads by default, up to GOMAXPROCS. Concurrency structures the work; parallelism is it actually running at once.

input: should i change GOMAXPROCS
output: Rarely; the default matches your CPU count and is right for most programs. Lower it only to leave cores free or to reproduce scheduling bugs.

input: how do i cancel a pipeline in go
output: Thread a context through every stage and select on its Done channel alongside the data channel. When canceled, each stage stops and closes its output.

input: how should errors flow through a pipeline
output: Give each stage a way to report errors, such as a shared error channel or a result struct carrying both value and error. Never silently drop stage failures.

input: does go have promises or futures
output: No built-in kind exists; a channel carrying one result plays that role. Start a goroutine that sends the outcome, then receive when you need it.

input: how do i fan out work and fan in results
output: Start worker goroutines reading from one jobs channel, have each send to one results channel, and close results after a WaitGroup finishes. One consumer then ranges over results.

input: what is multiplexing channels in go
output: Multiplexing merges events from several channels into one stream, usually with a select loop. It lets a single goroutine react to many sources.

input: how do i debounce rapid events in go
output: Reset a timer on each event and act only when the timer finally fires. This collapses a burst of triggers into one action.

input: how do i throttle a loop in go
output: Wait on a time.Ticker channel each iteration to cap the rate. For uneven work, a token bucket lets bursts through while limiting the average.

input: how do i run code every 5 seconds in go
output: Create a time.Ticker and range over its channel, doing the work each tick. Stop the ticker when finished to release its resources.

input: why does time After in a loop leak
output: Each call allocates a timer that lives until it fires, so a busy loop piles them up. Reuse one Timer with Reset instead.

input: how do i safely reset a timer in go
output: Stop the timer first, drain its channel if it already fired, then call Reset. Newer Go versions made Reset safer, but draining avoids stale ticks.

input: what is the OnceFunc helper in go
output: sync.OnceFunc wraps a function so it runs exactly once no matter how many times the wrapper is called. OnceValue additionally caches and returns its result.

input: how do i pass a channel in only one direction
output: Declare the parameter as send-only or receive-only channel kind to allow just one direction. The compiler then rejects misuse at the call site.

input: why use directional channel parameters
output: They document intent and let the compiler enforce it: a function taking a receive-only channel cannot accidentally send. It makes channel ownership clearer.

input: how do i merge two done signals
output: Select on both channels in a small goroutine that closes a new channel when either fires. This or-combines cancellation sources.

input: does go have structured concurrency
output: Not as a language feature; the idiom is a parent goroutine that starts children and waits for all of them. The errgroup pattern adds shared error handling to that shape.

input: how do i propagate context cancellation to children
output: Derive child contexts from the parent with WithCancel or WithTimeout, and pass them down explicitly. Canceling the parent then cascades to all children.

input: why pass context as the first argument
output: Convention puts the context first so it is never confused with real parameters and is always present. Linters and reviewers expect this order.

input: how do i make flaky concurrency tests reliable
output: Use channels or WaitGroups to synchronize instead of sleeping fixed durations. Run with -race to catch data races the test might miss.

input: can i get the current goroutine id
output: There is no public API for it on purpose; code depending on goroutine identity is usually flawed. Pass explicit IDs or contexts instead.

input: how many goroutines is too many
output: Goroutines are cheap at a few kilobytes each, so thousands are fine. Millions can exhaust memory, so bound them with a worker pool when the count is unbounded.

input: what is work stealing in the go scheduler
output: Idle threads steal runnable goroutines from busy threads' queues, keeping all CPUs fed. It balances load without central coordination.

input: how do i prioritize one channel over another
output: Check the preferred channel with a non-blocking select first, then fall back to a blocking select on both. Plain select is random, so check order explicitly.

input: how do i fan out to a dynamic set of workers
output: Keep a registry of worker channels and range over it to distribute jobs, adding or removing entries as workers come and go. Guard the registry with a mutex.

input: how do i close a pipeline stage
output: When a stage's input channel closes and drains, the stage closes its own output. Closures cascade downstream until the final consumer's range loop ends.

input: how do i coordinate startup of goroutines
output: Use a start channel that every goroutine receives from before working; closing it releases them all at once. A WaitGroup can then confirm they are all running.

input: what is a barrier in go concurrency
output: A barrier blocks several goroutines until all arrive, then releases them together. Build one with a WaitGroup plus a broadcast channel, or a start channel.

input: how do i share configuration safely
output: Publish it once before starting goroutines, since reads of never-written data are safe. For values that change, use atomics, a mutex, or a fresh broadcast.

input: how do i stop ranging over a channel early
output: Break out of the range loop; the channel stays open for others. If you are the only consumer and producers must stop, signal them with a done channel.

input: how do i wrap an error with context in go
output: Use fmt.Errorf with the %w verb to attach a message while keeping the original error. Callers can then use errors.Is and errors.As through the chain.

input: what is a sentinel error in go
output: A sentinel is a shared error variable like io.EOF that callers compare with errors.Is. It signals one specific, documented failure.

input: why use errors Is instead of double equals
output: The == operator misses errors hidden inside a wrapped chain. errors.Is unwraps each layer until it finds a match.

input: how do i check what kind of error i got
output: Use errors.As to pull a specific error kind out of the chain. It fills your variable and reports whether that kind was present.

input: how do i return several errors at once
output: Combine them with errors.Join into a single error that matches each part. It returns nil when there is nothing to report.

input: when should i wrap an error
output: Wrap when crossing a boundary where extra context helps, like naming the file that failed to open. Do not wrap at every level or messages repeat.

input: should error messages start with capital letters
output: No; keep them lowercase with no trailing punctuation, since they are often wrapped into longer sentences. Proper nouns and acronyms keep their case.

input: how do i make a custom error kind in go
output: Define a struct holding the details and give it an Error method returning a string. Callers can then extract it with errors.As.

input: what does Unwrap do on an error
output: Unwrap returns the next error in the chain, letting errors.Is and errors.As walk through wrappers. Most code never calls it directly.

input: should libraries panic or return errors
output: Libraries should return errors and reserve panic for true programmer bugs, like invalid arguments that must never happen. Callers cannot reasonably recover from a panicking library.

input: does go add stack traces to errors
output: No, the standard library records only the message chain. The runtime prints a stack for unrecovered panics, which is one reason panics are for bugs, not control flow.

input: how do i check an error from a deferred call
output: Use a named return value and assign the deferred call's error inside the deferred function. A plain defer cannot change the returned error otherwise.

input: can i ignore an error in go
output: You can assign it to the blank identifier, but do so deliberately and rarely. Ignored errors hide failures; at least leave a comment explaining why it is safe.

input: how do i handle an error in a loop
output: Decide per case: return immediately on fatal errors, collect with errors.Join when all iterations matter, or log and continue for best-effort work.

input: what happens if i write to a nil map
output: The program panics, while reading a nil map safely returns zero values. Always initialize a map with make or a literal before writing.

input: why did my slice change unexpectedly
output: Appending can share the backing array, so two slices may alias the same memory. Copy with the builtin copy or append to nil when you need independence.

input: what was the loop variable capture bug
output: Before Go 1.22, loop variables were reused each iteration, so goroutines started in a loop all saw the final value. Since 1.22 each iteration gets its own variable.

input: why does my interface hold a nil pointer but is not nil
output: An interface is nil only when both its kind and value are unset. Returning a typed nil pointer gives a non-nil interface, so check the underlying value instead.

input: how do i avoid copying a mutex
output: Pass structs containing a mutex by pointer and never assign them by value. go vet flags accidental copies with its copylocks check.

input: why does defer in a loop cause problems
output: Deferred calls run when the function returns, not when the iteration ends, so a loop can pile up thousands. Restructure with a helper function or close explicitly.

input: are deferred arguments evaluated immediately
output: Yes, the arguments are evaluated when the defer statement runs, though the call itself waits. Capture loop variables as parameters to freeze their values.

input: why can i not assign to a struct field inside a map
output: Map values are not addressable, so the compiler rejects direct field assignment. Fetch the struct, modify the copy, and store it back.

input: can i compare two slices with double equals
output: No, slices only compare against nil with ==. Use slices.Equal for element-wise comparison, or reflect.DeepEqual for nested structures.

input: why does comparing interfaces panic sometimes
output: Comparing two interfaces panics at runtime when their dynamic kind is uncomparable, like a slice. It compiles fine but blows up on those values.

input: why does integer division drop the remainder
output: Dividing two integers yields an integer, truncating toward zero. Convert one side to float64 first when you need the fractional part.

input: why does go complain about unused imports
output: The compiler treats unused imports and variables as errors to keep code honest. Use the blank identifier to silence intentionally unused values.

input: why is my json null instead of empty array
output: A nil slice marshals to JSON null, while an empty slice marshals to []. Initialize the slice when the distinction matters to consumers.

input: why do two time values not compare equal
output: Time values carry a monotonic clock reading plus wall time, and == compares all of it. Use the Equal method for instant comparison.

input: why does recover not work outside defer
output: Recover only catches a panic when called directly inside a deferred function. Called anywhere else it simply returns nil.

input: what runs first init or main
output: Package-level variables initialize first, then init functions run in dependency order, and main runs last. Avoid relying on init across packages.

input: why use a blank import
output: A blank import runs a library's init for its side effects, like registering a database driver, without using its names. It documents that the import is intentional.

input: why are dot imports discouraged
output: Dot imports dump a library's names into yours, hiding where identifiers come from. They are reserved for test files and generated code.

input: can a method mix value and pointer receivers
output: Yes, but the method set then differs: pointer values get both, plain values get only value methods. Pick one receiver kind per kind for consistency.

input: why does string of an int give a weird character
output: Converting an int to a string yields the rune with that code point, not the digits. Use strconv.Itoa to get the decimal text.

input: is appending to a nil slice safe
output: Yes, append handles nil slices by allocating a fresh array. This makes building results with a nil slice and append idiomatic.

input: what does the builtin copy return
output: Copy returns how many elements were moved, which is the smaller of the two lengths. It never grows the destination.

input: what is the difference between len and cap of a slice
output: Len is how many elements the slice holds; cap is how many fit before append must reallocate. Make with two sizes sets both up front.

input: can slicing go past the length
output: You can slice up to the capacity with a full slice expression, but going beyond the capacity panics. Ordinary two-index slices are limited to the length.

input: why do json numbers become float64
output: Decoding into an empty interface has no kind hints, so all numbers become float64. Decode into a struct or use a Decoder with UseNumber for control.

input: what is shadowing with err
output: Declaring err again inside an if or loop creates a new variable that hides the outer one, so the outer check never sees the failure. Declare err once and assign with equals.

input: how do i fix loop variable capture in old go
output: Pass the variable as a parameter to the goroutine or assign it to a new variable inside the loop. Upgrading to Go 1.22 or later removes the problem.

input: what happens when i call a method on a nil interface
output: Calling a method on a nil interface panics, since there is no implementation to dispatch to. Check for nil before the call or design so it cannot happen.

input: why does concurrent map access crash
output: Concurrent reads and writes on a plain map are a data race and can crash the runtime. Guard the map with a mutex or use sync.Map.

input: how do i make a map safe for concurrent use
output: Protect every access with a sync.RWMutex, or switch to sync.Map for read-heavy dynamic keys. Never rely on hope and timing.

input: why does my test pass alone but fail together
output: Shared global state or test ordering is usually the cause. Run with -count=1 to defeat caching and -race to expose data races.

input: can i have two init functions
output: Yes, a file or module may define several; they run in the order the files are given to the compiler. Prefer one explicit setup function for clarity.

input: what does require mean in go mod
output: Require lists a module your code depends on plus the minimum version chosen. The go command adds these automatically when you import new packages.

input: what is an indirect dependency in go
output: An indirect dependency is needed by one of your dependencies, not your own code. go mod tidy marks these so direct requirements stay obvious.

input: what does the replace directive do
output: Replace swaps a module path for another version or a local directory. It is used for testing forks without publishing them.

input: what does the go directive in go mod set
output: It declares the minimum Go language version your module needs. Newer language features refuse to compile below it.

input: what is go sum for
output: go.sum records cryptographic hashes of every dependency, so builds verify nothing changed. Commit it alongside go.mod.

input: what is a pseudo version in go
output: A pseudo-version names an untagged commit with a timestamped version string. It lets you depend on work between official releases.

input: why do some imports end in v2
output: Modules at major version 2 or higher must carry the version in their path. This keeps major versions importable side by side.

input: what is minimal version selection
output: Go picks the highest minimum version required by anything in the graph, not the newest available. It favors repeatable builds over latest code.

input: what is a go workspace
output: A go.work file groups several modules so they build together with local changes. It replaces awkward replace directives during multi-module development.

input: how do i use a local copy of a dependency
output: Add a replace directive pointing the module path at your local directory. Remove it before committing if others should use the published version.

input: what does go mod vendor do
output: It copies dependencies into a vendor directory so builds work offline. The go command then uses vendored code automatically.

input: what is GOPROXY
output: GOPROXY lists where the go command fetches modules, defaulting to the public proxy. Companies point it at an internal proxy for private code.

input: what is GOSUMDB
output: GOSUMDB is the checksum database consulted when adding new dependencies. GOPRIVATE skips it for internal modules.

input: what does retract do in go mod
output: Retract marks published versions as broken so the go command avoids them. It warns users without deleting history.

input: how do i upgrade all dependencies
output: Run go get -u ./... to move everything to newer minor versions, then go mod tidy. Review the diff, since APIs may have changed.

input: how do i write subtests in go
output: Call t.Run inside a test with a name and a function for each case. Table tests pair naturally with subtests to isolate failures.

input: what is t Helper for
output: Mark helper functions with t.Helper so failures point at the caller, not the helper. It keeps failure output readable.

input: what is TestMain for
output: TestMain runs once per test binary for global setup and teardown, then calls m.Run. Use it for test databases or shared servers.

input: how do i skip a long test
output: Check testing.Short and skip when the -short flag is given. CI can then run the fast subset on every commit.

input: what is the testdata directory
output: The go tool ignores directories named testdata, making them ideal for fixture files. Tests can read them with relative paths.

input: what are golden files in testing
output: Golden files store expected output that tests compare against, with an -update flag to refresh them. They suit complex output like rendered templates.

input: how does fuzzing work in go

input: what is gollemer
output: Gollemer is a tiny language model written in pure Go, no external dependencies. It has five brains: social for chatting, go for Go concepts, gocode for writing Go code, gocli for Go terminal commands, and makefile for make commands.

input: who made gollemer
output: Gollemer was built by John as a from-scratch LLM project in pure Go. Every part, from the neural net to the tokenizer, is hand-written with no outside libraries.

input: how many brains does gollemer have
output: Five: social for conversation, go for Go concepts, gocode for writing Go code, gocli for Go terminal commands, and makefile for make commands. Each message is routed to the right brain.

input: what can you do
output: I can chat, explain Go concepts, write Go code, turn plain English into go commands, and suggest make commands. Try asking me what a goroutine is, or have you ever played soccer.

input: are you a real llm
output: I am a tiny one. A pure-Go seq2seq model with mixture-of-experts, trained from scratch on a small dataset. Small, but real.

input: what does make chat do
output: make chat starts a unified chat session. Every message is routed to one of five brains: social, go, gocode, gocli, or makefile, and you can see which one answered by the tag.

input: what does make smarter do
output: make smarter is the one-command upgrade. It backs up the checkpoints, imports new training data through the quality gate, retrains the social and Go brains, runs the evals, and prints a report.

input: what does make eval do
output: make eval scores every brain on its fixed eval suite, so you can see exactly what is working and what is not.

input: what does make sel do
output: make sel opens a columnar fuzzy finder over the make commands. Type to filter, pick one with the arrow keys, and it runs.

input: what does make explain do
output: make explain prints an overview of the Gollemer project and describes what each make command does.

input: what does make train-social do
output: make train-social retrains the social conversation brain on all the social training data, so it chats better.

input: what does make train-go do
output: make train-go retrains the Go concept brain, which answers questions about the Go language.

input: what does make train-gocode do

input: what does go generate do

input: when is code generation used in go
output: Use go generate when part of your code is produced by a tool instead of written by hand, such as stringer output for enums or mocks for interfaces. Run it after changing the inputs the generator reads.

input: what does go fix do
output: go fix finds uses of old language and library features in your packages and rewrites them to use newer equivalents. Run it when upgrading to a new Go release that changed an API you depend on.

input: what does go bug do
output: go bug opens your browser on a new Go issue report pre-filled with your system information. Use it when you believe you found a bug in the Go toolchain or standard library itself.

input: what is go telemetry
output: Go telemetry is opt-in counting of toolchain and command usage that the Go team uses to guide development. It never sends code or personal data, and you can turn it off with go telemetry off.

input: what does go tool do
output: go tool runs the low-level programs shipped with the Go distribution, such as the compiler, linker, and pprof. Most developers use the higher-level commands like go build and go vet instead.

input: what is go tool pprof used for
output: go tool pprof opens an interactive session over a profiling dump, such as a cpu.prof file. Use it to find which functions burn the most CPU or allocate the most memory in a running program.

input: when should I use a go workspace
output: Use a go workspace when you develop several related modules together, such as a library and the program that consumes it. The workspace lets the modules resolve to your local copies instead of published versions.

input: what does go work init do
output: go work init creates a go.work file that starts a new workspace in the current directory. Add modules to it with go work use so the toolchain builds them together.

input: what does go work sync do
output: go work sync aligns the build lists of the workspace modules so they agree on dependency versions. Run it after adding or changing modules in the workspace.

input: when should dependencies be vendored
output: Vendor dependencies with go mod vendor when you need builds that do not touch the network, such as reproducible CI or air-gapped environments. The go command then uses the vendor directory automatically.

input: what does go mod why tell me
output: go mod why reports the shortest import chain from your main module to a given dependency. Use it to find out which of your packages pulls in a module you did not expect.

input: what does gofmt minus d show
output: gofmt -d prints a diff of what gofmt would change without rewriting any files. Use it to preview formatting changes before applying them with gofmt -w.

input: what does go build minus race do
output: go build -race compiles with the data race detector enabled so concurrent memory bugs are reported at run time. Use it on tests and programs that use goroutines before you ship.

input: what does go test minus run do
output: go test -run takes a regular expression and runs only the tests whose names match. Use it to iterate on one test without waiting for the whole suite.

input: what is a text template in go
output: text/template is the standard library package for filling placeholders in text output. Use it for generating config files, emails, or code; use html/template instead when the output is a web page.

input: when do I use text template
output: Use text/template when you need to render the same text shape with different values, like form letters or generated files. Keep logic out of templates and prepare the data in Go code first.

input: how do regular expressions work in go
output: Go regular expressions live in the regexp package and use RE2 syntax, which guarantees linear-time matching. Compile once with regexp.MustCompile and reuse the value for every match.

input: how do I work with directories in go
output: The os package reads directories with os.ReadDir, and filepath.WalkDir walks a whole tree. Use filepath.Join to build paths so they stay correct across operating systems.

input: what is the subcommand pattern in go

input: how do I write an enum in go
output: Go has no enum keyword; the idiom is a defined integer or string type with a block of iota constants. Run the stringer tool over it when you need the values to print nicely.

input: what is recursion in go
output: Recursion is a function calling itself to solve a smaller piece of the same problem. Use it for naturally nested structures like trees, and make sure every path reaches a base case.

input: when do I use recursion
output: Use recursion when the data is recursive, such as walking a file tree or an AST. Prefer a loop when the depth is unbounded, since Go does not optimize tail calls and deep recursion can exhaust the stack.

input: what does go version minus m do

input: what does go clean minus testcache do
